description: We're a group of STEM students who love science, technology, and solving problems. We're here to learn, share ideas, and challenge ourselves by turning creative ideas into real solutions. We bring different skills, plenty of curiosity, and a willingness to try new things. Looking forward to building something cool together!
summary: PIRENTE is a mission-planning and navigation prototype that connects NASA terrain and rover observations with the decisions needed for human exploration of Mars. Focusing on Jezero crater, it combines mission planning, interactive mapping, 3D terrain and an astronaut visor. Users select scientific destinations, set mission constraints, compare shorter and lower-slope routes, and explore departure windows using historical environmental measurements. A linked elevation profile explains terrain difficulty, while a timeline shows mission progress and changing environmental readings. Users can then preview the route in 3D and follow projected guidance through an astronaut's first-person visor, with scientific information at each stop. By connecting orbital imagery, elevation, rover science and operational trade-offs in one workflow, PIRENTE addresses the Martian Map challenge and makes complex NASA resources actionable for exploration planning, training and education.
details:
What we developed

PIRENTE connects mission planning with an astronaut’s experience on the surface. Our working browser prototype addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge through a simulated expedition across a 2 × 2 km area of Jezero’s western delta.

NASA data in context

The terrain comes from Mars 2020 HiRISE imagery and elevation products, supported by CTX and THEMIS context layers. Perseverance waypoints anchor the scientific destinations, including Skinner Ridge and Wildcat Ridge. Rover photographs and published observations explain the science at each stop. Historical MEDA measurements provide air temperature, pressure and optical solar flux; a published Mastcam-Z record provides dust-opacity context.

Plan the expedition

Users select destinations and specify slope, distance, time, walking speed, work-at-stop and reserve constraints. A* searches a 5 m terrain grid, comparing shortest-distance and lower-slope alternatives while avoiding missing or over-steep terrain. Each itinerary includes the return to a hypothetical base. Slope-adjusted walking times use Tobler’s hiking function. A departure-time catalogue and a historical environmental window support scheduling. Monte Carlo simulations explore uncertainty in assumed speed, stop duration, delays and endurance use.

Understand the trade-offs

The interactive map combines imagery, relief, slopes, thermal context, scientific stops and clearly identified team interpretations. Routes can be compared against a linked elevation profile: moving over the chart identifies the corresponding point on the map. A timeline advances the simulated expedition and updates position, environmental readings and modelled endurance indicators.

Preview and follow the same route

The 3D view places the itinerary over measured relief and includes a route-following preview. The Visor provides a moving first-person scene, a ground-projected route, compass, minimap, turn guidance and destination information. When a waypoint is reached, its rover image and scientific task appear. This connects an orbital planning view with an understandable experience at ground level.

Creativity and intended impact

Our contribution is a continuous workflow from NASA observations to route comparison, scheduling, terrain preview and astronaut guidance. Scientific objectives remain connected to operational constraints. The prototype can support mission-concept exploration, training and education, helping users understand why a route or departure time may be preferable.

Tools and development

The application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet and Three.js. Python supports data preparation and Blender produces illustrative scene assets. The demonstration combines screen recordings of the working app, English narration and video composition. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex, Anthropic Claude and ElevenLabs assisted development and production, with disclosure of their roles.

Scope and assumptions

The EVA, habitat, shelter, suit parameters, radiation-dose estimates and success probabilities are simulations or team assumptions. MEDA observations describe a past sol, not a future forecast. Optical solar flux is distinct from ionizing radiation dose; space-weather feeds provide context rather than a Mars-specific exposure prediction. Added rocks, close-up textures and distant scenery are illustrative.
